Merav Bar November 11, 2026 | 2 minute read A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE). As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. What is CVE-2026-119618? CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team. Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process. That’s according to Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) input output tables. An hour of work in American business now makes two and a half times what it made in 1973. For every forty hours that used to be needed, twenty-four have been freed. You have probably not noticed them. The forty-hour week was written into American law by an act of 1938, and hasn’t changed. Counted for each head of population, the hours worked in American business in 2024 were 10 percent higher than in 1973. As a country, the US took the whole of fifty years’ progress as more output and none of it as time. It was supposed to go differently. In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes wrote a short essay about the world his grandchildren would live in. He predicted that “the standard of life in progressive countries one hundred years hence will be between four and eight times as high as it is to-day.” And with so much plenty, he thought, we would hardly need to work at all: “Three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week” would be enough. He is usually said to have been right about the wealth and wrong about the leisure. Output per person in the United States in 2024 was 7.8 times its level in 1930. page.text_excerpt: Machine Learning Research Overview Research Highlights Publications Events Work with us Content Type Highlight published November 5, 2026 Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently. Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming. In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.1 Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself. Thinking loops# Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops, repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer. On top of this fleet we run a set of platform services that provides services for things like identity management, application deployment, and observability across the fleet. In addition, we also manage hundreds of thousands of internet of things (IOT) devices such as fryers, grills, or tablets (user interfaces) that send billions of MQTT messages each month in addition to operational metrics and logs. Operating 2,800+ discreet footprints of Kubernetes is not without its challenges. The same is true for any of the edge applications deployed by our internal teams, which are customers of the platform. Anyone running an application needs strong observability capabilities and this is certainly true at the Edge, too. In this post, we’ll share about our observability architecture for the edge at Chick-fil-A. Challenges at the Edge The edge brings a lot of unique challenges and constraints that are somewhat foreign to the modern cloud native mindset. Logging: There are simply too many application logs to push debug from every Kubernetes pod and IOT device to the cloud in realtime. I. Throughout Capital and the Grundrisse, Marx makes clear the profoundly contradictory nature of technology under capitalism and what he calls the “civilising tendency of capital”. Capitalism, it can’t be denied, has seen profound technological advancements in machinery, transport, communication, medicine, etc. Capital, though, did not produce any of these advancements. Human knowledge and labour did. Capital, in search of a larger profit, simply organised this human knowledge and labour to do its scientific work to make and then put into actions these innovations—not because these innovations were good for society in some way, but because they would be profitable. The ‘civilising tendency’ of capital is a by-product, a happy accident, of capital’s endless thirst for profit. But it plays a critical historical role all the same. A consequence of this is that workers, gradually over time, alongside their increasing exploitation by capital, gain access to more use-values, to more things. Vehicles, televisions, smartphones, videogames, medicine gradually shift over time (as their capitalist owners require more profit) from specialist things accessed only by a few elite, to things that that a much larger group of people are able to access. What was previously a luxury item becomes, over time, perceived as a necessary item all people deserve access to. Of course, the quality of the things we get reduce in quality at the same time as they are made under more standardised and cost-cutting conditions. Again, none of this is the purpose of capitalism. page.description: AWS Nitro Sandboxes is a new Amazon EC2 building block that gives each container, EKS pod, or ECS task the boundary of a hardware-isolated virtual machine, bringing the Nitro System's strong isolation, zero operator access, and cryptographic attestation to container workloads at near-native performance.
page.text_excerpt: Skip to Main Content AWS Blogs Home Blogs Editions AWS Compute Blog Nitro Sandboxes: Hardware isolation for every EKS pod, ECS task, and EC2 workload by Alex Graf on 10 NOV 2026 in Amazon EC2, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service, Announcements, Expert (400) Permalink Share Security has been the foundation of AWS cloud computing since day one. When we built Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), we designed it with strong isolation that keeps customer workloads and data separated from every other tenant on the same hardware. The AWS Nitro System took that further by moving virtualization, storage, and networking onto dedicated hardware, making zero operator access to customer data the default. Customers then asked us for more. They wanted tightly scoped, attestable environments for their most sensitive processing: the code and data that required protection even from their own administrators. That’s why we built Nitro Enclaves. Today, more of those sensitive workloads run in containers on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), and self-managed Kubernetes and container runtimes on Amazon EC2. Customers are asking for the same level of isolation and confidentiality for container environments. Container environments today host many independent workloads on a single EC2 instance by using Linux container technology. For a lot of customers, Linux containers have become the prevalent workload delivery vehicle because of their ease of deployment and the ability to have them share resources in one host through a shared kernel. This sharing has some downsides. Operators of a shared cluster have access to all the tasks running in it. A weakness in the shared kernel reachable by one container also exposes every other container on the host.
